Metaphorically 'to betray', about which Harpocration p. 259, 11: προπεπωκότες [having betrayed]: instead of προδεδωκότες [having betrayed]; it is said metaphorically. At the beginning of the Myrmidons Aeschylus (fr. 128): τάδε μὲν λεύσσεις, φαίδιμ᾽ Ἀχιλλεῦ, δοριλυμάντους Δαναών μόχθους, οὓς ** εἴσω κλισίας [You see these things, glorious Achilles, the spear-wasted toils of the Danaans, whom ** within the tent]. The first verse is cited by Aristophanes Frogs 1023, where the scholiast says: 'It is the beginning of the Myrmidons of Aeschylus.' Blomfield supplies σὺ προπίνεις [you betray] in the Preface to the Persians p. XII, προπεπωκώς [having betrayed] Heath, which word can be had if in the beginning of the verse the second person of some verb is read, such as θάσσεις [you sit]. Other examples in the Thesaurus vol. 6 p. 1815.
